overview: This file consists of a one-page “List of Papers” for State Department file 894.8593 on fueling and fuel-station policy toward Japanese merchant vessels in 1941. The index describes four underlying papers concerning British and American efforts to restrict Japanese ships in South and Central America, the South Atlantic, Buenos Aires, and Singapore to only the coal, oil, water, or bunkering facilities needed to reach their next port, partly to prevent supplies from reaching enemy raiders. It records diplomatic discussions involving the British Embassy, Under Secretary of State Sumner Welles, British Ambassador Lord Halifax, Assistant Secretary Adolf A. Berle Jr., and an official whose OCR-rendered surname is “Petion.”

subfiles.title: List of Papers on Fueling and Fuel Stations—Japan
subfiles.about: An index summarizes four papers on restricting fuel and other supplies furnished to Japanese vessels in the Americas and Singapore.
subfiles.summary: The sheet lists a British Embassy proposal of July 29 for coordinated British-American action to deny bunkering facilities to Japanese vessels in South and Central America. It also records Sumner Welles’s July 28 conversation with Lord Halifax about Japanese ships in the South Atlantic and Adolf A. Berle Jr.’s August 1 concern that discouraging Buenos Aires coal dealers might provoke resentment. A March 19 Singapore memorandum reports instructions to limit Japanese vessels to the oil, coal, and water required to reach their next port, with apparent Dutch cooperation, in order to prevent supplies from reaching enemy raiders.

interest: The index is useful for reconstructing the coordination of British and American maritime economic pressure on Japan around the 1941 asset freeze, even though the underlying papers are absent from the surviving OCR. Particularly revealing are Berle’s concern about Argentine sensitivities and the Singapore report’s description of limiting ships to voyage-essential supplies. The page also points historians toward four distinct diplomatic records and shows how local commercial decisions about coal, oil, and water became instruments of wider wartime strategy.
